name: Lyric-Tempest
specific_features: Storm systems that produce electromagnetic emissions resembling musical patterns
Atmospheric microbial blooms visible as color changes in cloud bands
description: Lyric-Tempest is a massive gas giant whose atmospheric dynamics produce electromagnetic emissions that, when converted to audio frequencies, bear an uncanny resemblance to musical compositions. Banded circulation zones in shades of amber, cream, and deep burgundy wrap the planet in stripes visible from across the system. Persistent anticyclonic storms, some larger than terrestrial worlds, churn within and between these bands, their interaction generating the electromagnetic patterns that give the planet its name.

The upper atmosphere hosts microbial life, organisms that drift in the cloud decks metabolizing atmospheric compounds and reproducing in bloom cycles visible from orbit as shifts in cloud coloration. These blooms follow the storm patterns, thriving in the turbulent boundary zones where different atmospheric layers mix and nutrients become available. Their presence was initially mistaken for purely chemical phenomena until spectroscopic analysis revealed unmistakable biosignatures.

Deeper within Lyric-Tempest, conditions transition through extreme pressure and temperature regimes that current technology cannot directly observe. Models predict a metallic hydrogen layer beginning roughly thirty thousand kilometers below the visible cloud tops, and possibly a rocky core of significant mass at the planet's center. The electromagnetic music originates from interactions between the metallic hydrogen layer and the planet's powerful magnetic field, a natural radio broadcast powered by pressures that would crush any probe.

Helium-3 harvesting operations skim the upper atmosphere using automated collection platforms that ride the jet streams between circulation bands. The work is profitable but hazardous, as storm systems can develop with minimal warning and produce wind speeds that exceed the structural tolerances of collection equipment. The microbial blooms add a complication: some strains produce corrosive metabolic byproducts that degrade collection membranes, requiring frequent maintenance that eats into profit margins.
